infraspecific_note: Flora of North America recognizes three subspecies. Texas material is primarily treated as Asclepias tuberosa subsp. interior; older Texas treatments also discussed subsp. terminalis, which FNA now includes within subsp. interior.

range_verification.method: BONAP county map used as primary county-range authority; textual county data from USDA-derived 2026 distribution data used to cross-check target-zone counties.
range_verification.note: Those counties were present in the earlier working record but are not in the current USDA-derived Texas county list consulted during this curation pass.

morphology_keys.sap_type: Clear to watery sap; notably lacks the typical milky latex of most Asclepias.
morphology_keys.stem: Stout, clustered from the crown, erect to spreading, conspicuously hairy/pilose.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Alternate; leaves often crowded and can appear irregularly approximate.
morphology_keys.leaf_morphology: Highly variable; narrow-lanceolate to broadly oblanceolate/oblong-lanceolate, usually 3–12 cm long, short-petiolate to nearly sessile, surfaces conspicuously hairy.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Terminal to subterminal branching system bearing several- to many-flowered umbelliform cymes; overall cluster often rounded to flat-topped.
morphology_keys.flower_color: Usually vivid orange; yellowish or reddish forms can occur.
morphology_keys.gynostegium_detail: Orange to yellowish gynostegium; corona hoods contain horns. Corolla lobes are reflexed.
morphology_keys.fruit: Elongate follicle, gray-green to brownish, with short hairs; seeds comose.

fastest_traits: Clear/watery sap rather than milky latex
field_diagnostics.best_field_combo: Orange Asclepias flowers + alternate hairy foliage + clear sap is an unusually strong field combination in Texas.

similar_species.distinction: Tropical milkweed normally has milky latex and opposite, smoother leaves; its flowers are typically red/orange with yellow hoods.

field_diagnostics.texas_milkweed_guide_note: TPWD calls the species very distinct and notes no close Texas look-alike based on its bright orange flowers and lack of milky sap.

ecological_notes.habitat: Blackland and coastal prairies, Crosstimbers, Grand Prairie, post oak and pine-oak savannas, sandy terraces/sandhills, open woods, hillsides, and other sunny well-drained sites.
ecological_notes.soil: Well-drained sand, loam, clay, limestone, and other dry to mesic mineral soils.
ecological_notes.host_status: Larval host for monarchs, but Texas sources describe it as a less-preferred or limited host compared with some other native milkweeds; flowers are valuable nectar resources.
ecological_notes.drought_adaptation: Deep root system supports strong drought tolerance once established.
